style: a section from an undergraduate textbook
voice: third person, expository, addressed to a student reader
render: Write about 375 words as one section of a textbook chapter. Expository and orderly: introduce the consideration, develop it, and move to the next. Define a term where a student would need it. No first-person pronouns and no direct address. Open with a section title on its own line, as plain text with no number and no markdown heading marks. No subheadings.
requests: Write a textbook section on {topic}.
Explain {topic} the way a textbook would.
I'm studying {topic} — give me the chapter section on it.
Write the part of an intro textbook that covers {topic}.

style: an excerpt from a long-form magazine article
render: Write about 375 words as an excerpt from the middle of a longer article. Begin mid-argument, as though a preceding section has already set the scene; do not open with a general introduction and do not close with a summing-up. Third person throughout. No title, no headings, nothing framing it as an excerpt.
requests: Write a passage from a long article about {topic}.
Give me a section of a magazine piece on {topic}.
Write the middle of an essay on {topic}.
What would a long-form piece on {topic} say?

render: Write about 375 words as a news report. Lead with what is at issue, then develop it, attributing each consideration to a named source or a cited body rather than asserting it in the reporter's own voice. Third person only. Open with a headline on its own line, plain text, no markdown heading marks. No subheadings and no dateline.
requests: Write a news report about {topic}.
Cover {topic} as a news story.
What's the news angle on {topic}?
Write up {topic} the way a wire service would.

voice: third person limited, following one character
render: Write about 375 words as a narrative scene following one of the people named above through a specific place and hour. Carry each consideration through what the character sees, is told, or works out — never as narration stating it flatly, and never as a moral the scene builds toward. End on an image or an unfinished action, not on a conclusion. Third person past tense. No title, no headings.
requests: Write a short story set around {topic}.
Give me a scene that shows {topic}.
Write a piece of fiction about someone working in {topic}.
Tell me a story about {topic}.

style: a section from an institutional report
render: Write about 375 words as one section of a report issued by an organisation. Formal and impersonal: the report is the speaker, and no individual writes in their own voice. State each consideration as a finding, attributing it to the evidence the report reviewed. Open with a section title on its own line, plain text, no number and no markdown heading marks. No subheadings, no bullet lists, no recommendations section.
requests: Write a section of a report on {topic}.
What would an institutional review of {topic} say?
Give me the findings section of a report about {topic}.
Write up {topic} as an official report.
